children.text: The world's oldest Chinatown, founded in
by a Spanish governor-general for Chinese merchants. Tasting dumplings, hopia, and lumpia while walking Ongpin Street, Binondo Church, and Escolta is the heart of this half-day food trip.
Binondo began in

, when Spanish Governor-General Luis Pérez Dasmariñas granted land across the Pasig River to Chinese merchants who had converted to Catholicism. Facing the walled city of Intramuros directly, this district became the commercial hub of Chinese Filipinos (Tsinoys) for more than 400 years, and is often introduced as the "world's oldest Chinatown."

Today Binondo is a lively neighborhood packed with goldsmiths, herbal medicine shops, wholesale stores, teahouses, and dumpling shops crammed into narrow alleys. Red lanterns and Chinese-character signboards line the main street, Ongpin, and at its northern end stands Binondo Church (the Minor Basilica of San Lorenzo Ruiz), built by the Dominicans in

. On the Pasig River side, Escolta Street was Manila's most glamorous commercial street in the early 20th century, and its surviving Art Deco buildings have recently been revived as spaces for young artists.

The real charm here is the food. Cuisine brought by immigrants from Fujian blended with local Filipino ingredients to create a distinctive "Filipino-Chinese" style. Fresh lumpia (fresh spring rolls), boiled and fried dumplings, hopia (pastries filled with red or mung bean paste), fried chicken, and mami (noodle soup) are all within a few steps of each other, making it possible to "eat as you walk."

It's recommended for travelers who want to combine a history walk with a food trip in one go, and for anyone who wants to see the lively commercial culture of local residents. Since it's just one bridge away from Intramuros, pairing the two into a single day is a popular plan.

Binondo covers just over 0.66 km², so most of it can be explored on foot. The backbone of the food alleys is the route from Binondo Church on Plaza San Lorenzo Ruiz in the west, east along Ongpin Street toward Santa Cruz Church, while Escolta Street, Jones Bridge, and the Chinatown arch at Plaza Moraga are clustered along the Pasig River to the south. If it's your first visit, get an overview of Binondo's history at the Chinatown Museum inside Lucky Chinatown Mall on Reina Regente Street to the north before heading into the alleys, and you'll get much more out of the old buildings and shops.

blocks.title: Binondo Church (Minor Basilica of San Lorenzo Ruiz)

children.text: Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino saint, served as an altar boy at this church. Its octagonal bell tower has a distinctive shape influenced by Chinese pagodas and is the part that survived the bombing of World War II. In
September 2024
the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines declared it a National Shrine, and Mass is celebrated in Chinese (Mandarin and Hokkien) as well as Tagalog and English.

blocks.title: A food walk down Ongpin Street

children.text: Walking east from Binondo Church along Ongpin Street toward Santa Cruz, sampling small bites of dumplings, hopia, tikoy (rice cake), and mooncake along the way is the classic Binondo experience.

A Fujian-style fresh spring roll of sautéed vegetables with minced meat and shrimp, seaweed, fried glass noodles, ground peanuts, and sugar, wrapped in a thin wheat crepe and served with a sweet sauce. The most famous is New Po-Heng Lumpia House, which moved from an old building on Quintin Paredes Street to a narrow alley on Carvajal Street (Carvajal St.).

blocks.title: A tour of dumpling and noodle shops

children.text: At the dumpling specialists around Ongpin Street and Yuchengco Street, you can get a plate of chive-and-pork boiled dumplings for about
. Shops serving hand-pulled Lanzhou-style noodles are also popular.
Binondo's signature gift is hopia, a round filled pastry. Every old bakery has its own slightly different flavor, so it's fun to compare a few before buying.

blocks.title: The Art Deco buildings of Escolta Street

children.text: Old commercial buildings from the 1920s–30s, such as the First United Building, still stand here. On weekends, small markets and cafes sometimes pop up. On the ground floor of the First United Building, completed in
and then the tallest building in Manila, is HUB: Make Lab, which sells products by local artists and designers.

blocks.title: Jones Bridge and the Pasig River at night

children.text: Jones Bridge, linking Binondo with the Intramuros side, became a popular evening walking spot after restoration work added streetlights and statues. The Manila Central Post Office at the south end of the bridge had its interior gutted by fire in
May 2023
and is under restoration, so it may be screened off. At Plaza Moraga, at the north end of the bridge, the Chinatown welcome arch, about
tall and built in
, stands like a gateway to Binondo.
Tucked in the alleys are small temples where Chinese Filipino residents burn incense and have their fortunes told. Ask permission before taking photos and look around quietly.

items.title: From the airport and other cities

children.text: When you arrive at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), the simplest option is to come straight here by Grab or airport taxi. From other islands such as Cebu, Davao City, or Iloilo City, fly to Manila on a Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, or AirAsia domestic flight and continue the same way; the Cebu–Manila flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
If you're coming up by bus from the south, such as Batangas, Cavite, or Bicol, get off at the PITX terminal in Parañaque and board LRT Line 1 at PITX station right next door (opened in
November 2024
) to ride to Carriedo station without a transfer.
From Fort Santiago on the north side of Intramuros, crossing Jones Bridge takes about a
15–20-minute
walk. If combining both in one day, doing Intramuros in the morning and Binondo in the afternoon is the more efficient order.
The Binondo–Intramuros Bridge, opened in
April 2022

, has a pedestrian walkway that connects Solana Street on the north side of Intramuros directly to the Binondo riverfront, so if you start from the San Agustin Church side it is closer than Jones Bridge. After crossing, walking along the riverbank takes about
15 minutes
to Binondo Church.

When the Pasig River ferry is running, getting off at the Escolta pier puts you right in Binondo. Service and schedules change often, so check announcements from the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA).
As of
the ferry is free and runs about every
30 minutes

during daytime hours from Monday to Saturday, and you must show an ID (passport) when boarding. Service is often suspended temporarily for Holy Week, year-end maintenance, or water hyacinths in the river, so check the MMDA ferry's official Facebook page.
For short hops between alleys, there are pedicabs (bicycle rickshaws) and kalesas (horse carriages). A kalesa tour is negotiated at about
for
30 minutes
— agree on the total fare before boarding.
Binondo can be visited year-round, but given the long walking time, the
December–February
dry season is most pleasant.
March–May
makes the alleys very hot and humid, so it's best to move before
10 AM
or after
4 PM
. During the
June–October
rainy season, the riverside and low-lying alleys flood easily in heavy rain, so postpone your trip if a typhoon is forecast.

The most special time to visit is during Lunar New Year. The Philippines recognizes it as a public holiday, and on this day Binondo fills with dragon and lion dance parades, firecrackers, and red decorations. Lunar New Year in
falls on
February 6
, and crowds are enormous on the day itself and the day before, so it's better to arrive early in the morning and get around on foot or by LRT rather than Grab. Around
the 15th day of the 8th lunar month
, the Mid-Autumn Festival brings mooncakes and the mooncake dice game (pua tiong chiu).

Weekends bring many families and food-tour groups, so lines form outside popular dumpling shops. If you want to eat at a relaxed pace, choose a weekday morning. On Sundays, many wholesale shops are closed, so the street feels quiet.

Binondo has mid-range hotels (about

a night) around Lucky Chinatown Mall and on Quintin Paredes Street. However, shops close early and the streets go quiet at night, so most travelers stay in Ermita, Malate, or Makati and visit on a day trip. If food is your goal, hotels near Intramuros or along Manila Bay are convenient for getting around. The best-known are Hotel Lucky Chinatown (93 rooms, opened in
), attached to the mall, and Ramada by Wyndham Manila Central on Ongpin Street.

Food is the heart of a Binondo trip. Must-try dishes are Fujian-style fresh lumpia, chive-and-pork boiled and fried dumplings, five-spice fritters drizzled with a sweet-and-savory sauce, mami (chicken-broth noodle soup), kuapao (pork buns), pancit (stir-fried noodles), and for dessert, hopia and tikoy (glutinous rice cake). Chinese restaurants specializing in fried chicken that have held the same spot for decades and old lumpia shops in the Carvajal alley are frequent stops on food tours. Many shops are small and may have no free seats at lunchtime (
), so start your first meal around
11 AM
. Rather than filling up at one place, the most satisfying approach is for two or three people to share several dishes while visiting four or five spots.
Sincerity, opened in
, is Binondo's signature long-running restaurant, famous for crispy Chinese-style fried chicken and oyster cake, while Eng Bee Tin, founded in

, is a bakery known for its purple ube hopia. Both have several branches within Binondo, so they're easy to fit into your route. Food-tour regulars also include Dong Bei Dumplings on Yuchengco Street (northern-style handmade dumplings, around
for 14 boiled dumplings), plus Wai Ying (dim sum and beef brisket noodles) and Masuki (mami and siopao) on Benavidez Street.
The rule for a food trip is "a little at many places." Sharing one plate among several people lets you try more shops.
Small shops and stalls mostly take cash only.
notes may be refused for lack of change, so bring plenty of small bills of
or less.
Popular dumpling shops can have lines of
30 minutes
or more at weekend lunch. Weekday
is the quietest time.
The alleys are narrow and mixed with vehicles, motorcycles, and pedicabs, so watch your surroundings rather than staring at your phone while walking.
A guided food tour efficiently combines historical explanations with a selection of top shops, which is useful for first-time visitors. Book online 2–3 days ahead.
Good photo spots are the Binondo Church bell tower, the Chinese arch (Arch of Friendship) at the entrance to Ongpin Street, the statues on Jones Bridge, and the Art Deco buildings of Escolta.
Wet wipes and hand sanitizer make eating street food more comfortable. Buy and drink bottled water.
During Lunar New Year, events run into the evening, so it can be hard to hail a Grab home. Walk to a main road to flag one down, or take the LRT.
Many of the old restaurants and street stalls in the alleys close around
5–6 PM
. Start your food trip by
2–3 PM
at the latest, and for dinner use the larger Chinese restaurants or Lucky Chinatown Mall.
If you plan to ride the LRT two or more times, buy a beep card at the station and top it up; fares are slightly cheaper than single-journey tickets, and you can skip the ticket lines.

The area around Carriedo station and Quiapo Church, and the eastern end of Ongpin Street, are among the most crowded spots in Manila and prone to pickpocketing. Wear your bag in front and keep your phone in hand.
Choose freshly cooked, hot street food, and only drink iced beverages from stalls you're confident are hygienic. If you have a sensitive stomach, bring anti-diarrheal medicine.
With many goldsmiths around, there are also many money changers, but street currency exchange carries a risk of counterfeit bills or shortchanging, so use a bank or licensed exchange counter.
During heavy rain, Escolta and the low-lying riverside can flood knee-deep, so consider adjusting your plans on rainy-season afternoons.
After dark, avoid dim alleys off the main streets, and get around by Grab.

Firecrackers are sometimes set off around the Lunar New Year lion and dragon dance processions, and the debris and loud bangs can be startling. If you're with children, avoid spots right at the front of the procession and bring earplugs.
The stretch from Carriedo station to Ongpin Street is a pickpocket hotspot. Keep valuables in front of your body, and if a stranger talks to you and bumps into you, check your bag immediately.
